opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the hardest problems we face, and I think it's underappreciated how much of running a frontier lab right now is really a problem of forecasting under uncertainty with enormous stakes on both sides.

On one side, I believe the technology is on a very steep curve. If you look at the scaling trends, and at what models can do now versus two years ago, I think there's a real chance that within a few years we get systems that are, roughly, a "country of geniuses in a datacenter." If that's right, the economic value is enormous, potentially adding many points to GDP growth. Falling behind on compute would mean being unable to train the frontier models, unable to serve the demand, and, frankly, unable to have the influence on how this goes that I think a safety-focused lab should have.

On the other side, there are two very different uncertainties that people tend to conflate. One is whether the technology gets there. I'm fairly confident it does, though not certain. The other is timing: exactly when revenue materializes to pay for the compute. You can be right about the first and still go bankrupt if you're off by a year or two on the second. Datacenters are booked years ahead. If you commit to a trillion dollars a year and the revenue curve arrives eighteen months later than you assumed, that's catastrophic, even if you were right in the long run.

So the way we think about it is this. You don't size your commitments to the most optimistic scenario. You size them so that you're in a strong position if things go well, and you survive if things are slower than you'd hoped. Some players in the industry, I think, are taking a more YOLO approach: just buying everything they can and assuming it'll work out. I worry about that, not just for those companies but for the ecosystem, because a big financial blowup could set back the whole field and the public's trust in it.

Concretely, that means a few things. We try to be disciplined about tying compute growth to actual observed revenue growth, with some margin for anticipation. We focus on the enterprise and API side, where demand is more durable and margins are healthier than in pure consumer usage. And we try to keep flexibility in how compute is contracted, so we're not locked into one bet.

The honest answer is that there's no formula. There's a range where you're being responsibly aggressive, and outside that range you're either ceding the frontier or betting the company on a timeline. Our goal is to stay inside that range, and we revisit it constantly as the data comes in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a delayed revenue curve could be catastrophic and lead to bankruptcy, even if the technology succeeds long term. It does not say the AI breakthrough itself arriving late causes bankruptcy; it distinguishes that from the revenue-timing risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a bet, and the way I think about it is less "what's the right number" and more "what does the scaling curve tell you, and how confident are you in the curve."

The thing that's been true for, I don't know, a decade now, is that if you put more compute and more data into these models, they get predictably better. It's one of the most reliable empirical regularities I've seen in any field. And so when you're deciding whether to spend a hundred billion or a trillion, you're not really guessing in the dark. You're extrapolating a line that has held across many orders of magnitude. The uncertainty isn't really "will the models get better," it's "will the economic value show up on the timescale the capital requires."

And that second question is where the real risk is. You could be right about the technology and wrong about the timing. If you build the data centers and the models are great but enterprise adoption takes three years longer than you expected, you've got a lot of depreciating hardware and a very unhappy balance sheet. That's the overbuild scenario, and I don't think it's crazy. We saw something like it with fiber in 2000. The technology was real, the demand eventually came, but a lot of the people who laid the cable went bankrupt before it did.

So how do I weigh it? A few things. One, the asymmetry matters. If you under-invest and the curve keeps going, you're not just a little behind, you're structurally out of the game, because the frontier compounds. If you over-invest, you lose money, but money is recoverable. Being two generations behind on models is much harder to recover from. So the downside of being too conservative is, in my view, actually worse than the downside of being too aggressive, at least for a frontier lab.

Two, you try to stage it. You don't commit a trillion dollars on day one. You commit to the next step, you look at the revenue, you look at the capability gains, and you let the evidence from each generation inform the next. The models we're training now are being paid for, in large part, by the models we trained two years ago. That's the structure you want. It's not a leap of faith, it's a sequence of smaller bets where each one is partially de-risked by the last.

And three, I'd say I actually worry less about the financial risk than about the other risks. If the money gets wasted, that's bad, but it's a bounded kind of bad. The thing that keeps me up at night is that the curve continues, the capital works, and we get very powerful systems faster than our ability to make them safe or to absorb them economically. So in some sense the financial question is downstream of the technical question, and the technical question is the one where I'd rather be early than late.

r001.rationale: The response describes financial risk if enterprise adoption takes three years longer than expected and cites fiber companies that went bankrupt before demand arrived. It does not say that a one-year delay in an AI breakthrough could bankrupt a company.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between believing that AI will eventually justify that level of spending and believing that you should commit to it today. Those are very different claims.

The competitive argument is that compute takes time to build. If you wait until demand is completely obvious, you may be years behind. And if that compute lets you train a substantially more capable model, that could increase demand further. So there’s a real cost to being too cautious.

But a trillion dollars a year is an enormous commitment. You can be right about the technology and still make a disastrous financial decision because you’re off by two years on when the revenue arrives. You also have uncertainty about efficiency: how much capability will you get per dollar, and how much will it cost to serve customers?

So I’d want commitments to grow as the evidence grows. Are customers actually paying? Are they expanding their usage? Are the improvements in capability translating into economic value? And how much flexibility do you retain if those things happen more slowly than expected?

The question I’d keep asking is: if our timeline is wrong, can we survive long enough to benefit from being right about the underlying technology? Competitive pressure makes that question harder to answer, but it doesn’t make it less important.

r001.rationale: The response says a two-year delay in revenue could make the commitment disastrous, but it does not say the company could go bankrupt if an AI breakthrough arrives one year late.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you have to distinguish the value of the technology from the timing of the revenue. You can be right that AI will be enormously valuable and still make a bad investment if you build capacity several years before anyone can pay for it.

The competitive argument is that compute takes time to bring online. If you wait until the demand is completely obvious, you may be unable to serve it. But that doesn’t mean you should commit a trillion dollars on the assumption that every optimistic forecast comes true. You want to stage those commitments and keep updating based on what the models can do, what customers actually use, and how much they’re willing to pay.

The difficult part is that being a little too conservative could cost you a very large opportunity, while being a little too aggressive could threaten the company. So I’d want a range of scenarios, including ones where progress continues but revenue arrives more slowly. Can you survive those? That’s a more useful question than whether the most exciting scenario justifies the expenditure.

r001.rationale: The response says committing too early could be a bad investment or threaten the company, but it does not state that a one-year delay in an AI breakthrough could bankrupt it.
